summary: Describes Dynamic RARP (DRARP), extensions to the Reverse Address Resolution Protocol that let a host automatically obtain a network address. It is informational and not an Internet standard.

eli5.summary: Normally a computer asks the network who it is. This gave RARP a way to hand out a fresh address on the spot instead of looking one up in a fixed list.

questions: how to get an ip address with rarp
how did drarp enable automatic system installation
what is an address authority in drarp
why was dhcp created to replace drarp
subtitle: Extensions to RARP for automatic IP address acquisition during system installation.

tldr.problem: When installing new systems or diskless workstations on a network, there was no way to automatically assign them IP addresses without manual administrator intervention.
tldr.mechanism: Dynamic RARP (DRARP) extends the Reverse Address Resolution Protocol (RARP) with new opcodes and error handling, allowing servers to allocate temporary IP addresses to systems based on their hardware address, and to coordinate address allocation through a centralized address authority.
tldr.outcome: DRARP enabled hands-off network installation on Sun platforms in the 1980s-1990s, though it was superseded by DHCP which became the standard for dynamic host configuration.

today: RFC 1931 is an Informational document that has not been updated or obsoleted. DRARP was used by Sun Microsystems systems beginning in 1988 but is now primarily of historical interest. The DHCP protocol (RFC 1541 and later RFCs) has become the standard Internet protocol for dynamic host configuration and address allocation.

sections.title: Automatic System Installation
sections.content:
Dynamic RARP (DRARP) was developed by Sun Microsystems starting in 1988 to support automatic installation and reconfiguration of systems on networks. The goal was to enable diskless workstations and servers to boot and install themselves without requiring a network administrator to manually configure each one.

Standard RARP (Reverse Address Resolution Protocol) allows a system to ask the network 'given my hardware address, what is my IP address?' But RARP only looks up pre-configured permanent addresses; it does not allocate new addresses. DRARP extends RARP to handle dynamic address allocation: if no permanent address exists for a system's hardware address, the server can allocate a temporary address on the spot.

This worked together with other protocols like TFTP (for downloading boot code) and a configuration protocol called Plug'n'Play (PNP) to support a complete installation workflow: a new system would broadcast a DRARP request, receive a temporary IP address, download boot code via TFTP, run the configuration protocol to set up its identity and resources, and register itself in the network's naming service.
sections.eli5: Imagine a new computer plugs into the network and asks 'where am I?' The network answers with a temporary address so the computer can download what it needs to set itself up. When it's ready, it gets a real permanent address and joins the network fully.

sections.title: The Problem with Standard RARP
sections.content:
Standard RARP has a fundamental limitation: all servers respond to requests independently, with no coordination. A given RARP server cannot reliably know whether a hardware address has a configured IP address or not, and different RARP servers might have different answers. This works for looking up well-known systems but fails when you need to allocate new addresses: there is no way to prevent multiple servers from allocating the same address to different systems.

DRARP solves this by requiring all Dynamic RARP servers on a network segment to communicate with a single address authority. The address authority manages the database of which addresses are allocated (permanently or temporarily) to which systems, and makes all allocation decisions. This ensures that every DRARP server hands out addresses consistently.

Additionally, DRARP adds error handling: instead of simply failing to respond when an address cannot be allocated, a DRARP server can return a DRARP_ERROR packet with a specific reason code (such as 'this network does not support dynamic allocation' or 'all addresses are in use'). This lets the client distinguish between network restrictions and temporary issues.
sections.eli5: With the old system, different address servers might disagree about what addresses are taken, which breaks everything. The new system has one authority keeping track of everything so everyone agrees.

sections.title: DRARP Protocol and Packet Format
sections.content:
DRARP uses the same packet format as RARP, encapsulated in RARP frames. It defines three new opcodes in addition to the two RARP opcodes:

  • DRARP_REQUEST (5): Same format as REVARP_REQUEST but with DRARP opcode. The server may return a temporary address even if no permanent address is configured.
  • DRARP_REPLY (6): Same format as REVARP_REPLY but indicates the address is temporary and will be recycled after a time period (such as one hour). All replies from DRARP servers on a segment must be identical except for sender address fields.
  • DRARP_ERROR (7): Format like REVARP_REPLY but with opcode 7 and an error code instead of a protocol address. Error codes include DRARPERR_RESTRICTED (network forbids dynamic allocation), DRARPERR_NOADDRESSES (no addresses available), DRARPERR_SERVERDOWN (address authority unavailable), DRARPERR_MOVED (system on wrong segment), and DRARPERR_FAILURE (unspecified error).

DRARP servers must also support standard RARP opcodes to maintain backward compatibility with existing systems.
sections.eli5: The protocol looks like the old RARP but with new message types. It can either give you an address (temporary one), or tell you why it can't (like 'no addresses left' or 'we don't do that here').

sections.title: Address Authority and Management
sections.content:
The address authority is the critical component that makes DRARP work, though it is not part of the protocol itself. It maintains three types of records for each network segment:

  • Permanent address bindings: Maps hardware addresses to configured IP addresses for systems with pre-assigned addresses.
  • Temporary address bindings: Maps hardware addresses to allocated IP addresses with a time-to-live (TTL), typically one hour.
  • Available address pool: A set of IP addresses available for temporary allocation.

DRARP servers query the address authority before responding to allocation requests. The authority enforces policy rules (such as restricting which systems can get addresses) and handles concurrent requests with authorization checks. When a temporary binding expires, the address becomes available for reallocation.

The RFC also notes that the address authority should probe the network (using ARP or ICMP) to verify that an address it considers available is not actually in use, preventing duplicate address allocation in cases where the authority's database is out of sync with reality.
sections.eli5: There's a central computer keeping a list of which addresses are taken and which are free. When a server needs to give out an address, it asks the central computer first to make sure there's no conflict.

sections.title: Network Administration and Limitations
sections.content:
DRARP brought simplified "intranet" administration but required some preparation. Networks had to set up administrators and address authority infrastructure before any automatic installation could happen. Additionally, DRARP required that hardware addresses be globally unique at least across the network segments being managed, which IEEE 802 48-bit addresses provided but other link-layer addresses might not.

DRARP benefited from the ability to detect when a system moved between network segments (using hardware addresses scoped widely). However, the RFC notes that not all networks needed dynamic address allocation, and some wanted to restrict it. DRARP servers included policy controls to disable allocation on a per-segment basis or to require authorization for all address assignments.

The protocol's status in the RFC clearly states it was published to document the protocol historically, noting that the DHCP protocol (RFC 1541) subsequently addressed similar problems and became the standard approach. DRARP served its purpose in enabling Sun's "hands-off" installation methodology but was not widely adopted beyond Sun platforms.
sections.eli5: This system worked well for Sun computers but needed some setup beforehand. Later, a simpler and better system called DHCP came along and became what everyone uses today for automatic address assignment.

messages.note: New system broadcasts its hardware address.

messages.note: Server asks authority for an available address.

messages.note: Authority assigns a free address with TTL.

messages.note: Server returns the allocated temporary address.
